title: tat tvam asi
tomorrow: a bird tied to a string flies off every way. where does it land?

segments.voice: Yesterday, tat tvam asi began with a proud son, a patient father and a lump of clay: many shapes, one clay. Today the father goes back to the very beginning, and meets an argument there.

Lights out at a sleepover, and somebody asks the question that ends all sleep. Before anything existed, was there something, or nothing? One voice says nothing. Another says you can't get something from nothing. Inside the Chandogya Upanishad, the same argument is already running, and Uddalaka pauses his son's lesson to take it on.
screen: `LIGHTS OUT. THE BIG QUESTION.` → `SOMETHING, OR NOTHING?` → `THE ARGUMENT IS ALREADY OLD.`

segments.voice: In the beginning, my dear, the father says, this was Being alone. One only, without a second. The word is sat: being, what is. Then he names the other view, fairly. Some say that in the beginning there was only non-being, and from non-being, being was born. That view has its own home in the tradition. Another Upanishad, the Taittiriya, says it in its own voice: in the beginning this was non-being, and from it being was born. Its best case goes like this. Before names and forms, there was no thing at all to point to, no this, no that; everything nameable came later. Uddalaka answers with a question. How could being come out of non-being? So, he says: in the beginning, Being alone, one without a second. And his Being doesn't sit still. It thought: may I be many, may I grow forth. It sent forth heat. Heat sent forth water, which is why, he says, a person who grieves or sweats grows wet. Water sent forth food, which is why rain brings a harvest. Some commentators read the Taittiriya's non-being as the not-yet-named, so the two lines can meet. Either way, the tradition kept both texts. And when the great saying comes, the that in that you are will point back here.
screen: `BEING ALONE, ONE WITHOUT A SECOND.` · `THE OTHER VIEW: NON-BEING FIRST.` · `MAY I BE MANY.` · then, large: `HEAT, WATER, FOOD.`

segments.voice: If there's paper near you, write two short lines by hand. In the beginning, being. In the beginning, non-being. Read each one slowly, as if it were your own view, and breathe between them without choosing.
Tat tvam asi: that you are. In the Chandogya, the that is Being, one without a second, whose first wish was to be many.
For the road: tat tvam asi, one without a second, wishing to be many. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers read Chandogya 6.2 alongside the Taittiriya's line on non-being, and commentators explain how the two fit; in study, both passages are heard as scripture.

match.prompt: two views of the beginning. tap the pairs.

myth: Hindu scriptures all give the same account of how everything began
the Chandogya says Being came first; the Taittiriya says non-being, then being. the tradition kept both.
Uddalaka links tears and sweat to heat
heat sent forth water, so when a person grieves or sweats, water comes from heat, he says.

fork.setup: at a debate club, you're told to argue the side you don't hold: in the beginning there was non-being. what's its best case?
options: before names and forms, there was no thing at all to point to.
no Hindu text ever says it, so there's no case to make.
it means the world is fake and nothing in it matters.
fork.reveal: the Taittiriya says it in its own voice: non-being first, then being. some commentators read non-being as the not-yet-named. Uddalaka answers it with a question.

original.note: Sanskrit: one only, without a second. The father's words for Being in the beginning.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hindu texts give one tidy answer to how it all began.
what it means: Uddalaka names the other view, non-being first, and answers it with a question.
what a scholar hears: sad eva somya idam agra asit, ekam evadvitiyam (Chandogya 6.2.1), beside asad va idam agra asit (Taittiriya 2.7.1).
recall: by it, every clay thing is known
the proud son who said: teach me

chat.says: Jess (co-counselor) says if everything began as 'one,' it must've been still and boring. is that Uddalaka's view?
options: no: his Being thought 'may I be many' and sent forth heat, then water, then food.
yes: Being stayed one and still, and nothing at all ever came out of it.
no: he says it all began as many separate things, never as one at all.
chat.meaning: In the Chandogya, Being alone, one without a second, wished to be many: it sent forth heat, heat sent forth water, water sent forth food.

Taittiriya.meaning: an Upanishad that says non-being came first

Uddalaka.meaning: the father teaching his son in the Chandogya

Chandogya Upanishad.meaning: the Upanishad where tat tvam asi is taught

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.2.1–4 (in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second; some say non-being, and being born from it; how could being be born from non-being?; Being thought, may I be many, may I grow forth, and sent forth heat; heat sent forth water, so when one grieves or sweats water comes from heat; water sent forth food, so wherever it rains food is plentiful)
Taittiriya Upanishad 2.7.1 (in the beginning this was non-being; from it being was born)

notes: Debate: the Taittiriya 2.7.1 line (asad va idam agra asit, tato vai sad ajayata) is given as the other view's own home. 'Some commentators read the Taittiriya's non-being as the not-yet-named' summarizes the reading of asat as the unmanifest (e.g., Shankara on Taittiriya 2.7); confirm the attribution and that the steelman ('no thing at all to point to') is fair.
